name: Producerism
summary: Producerism holds that those who make tangible wealth, such as farmers, artisans and wage workers, are the virtuous core of society and are exploited by idle or parasitic groups, above all bankers, monopolists, land speculators and aristocrats. It demands that government be taken back from corrupt elites and used to curb concentrated wealth through public money, public ownership of key networks and land for actual settlers. Critics note that the producer ideal was often racialized and gendered and that later strands aim the 'parasite' label at the poor below as well as elites above.
scope: The 19th-century American strand at its peak, as stated in its own texts: the Knights of Labor constitution (1878) and Powderly's history of the order, the People's Party Omaha platform (1892) and the 1891 Cincinnati demands, and the books of Populist leaders Weaver and Peffer. Modern right-populist uses (Perot, Buchanan, Trump, Le Pen) are not modelled, and the doctrine's texts are silent on most culture, religion and foreign-policy statements.
